title: Pradakshina
carry: keep the holy at the center
last: DARSHAN — SEEING GOD, AND BEING SEEN.

cards: Ganesha and his brother Kartikeya are told that whoever circles the world first wins. You met this race back on day twenty-five. Kartikeya jumps on his peacock and flies off across oceans and mountains.
Ganesha, on his little mouse, simply walks around his parents, Shiva and Parvati, and says: you are my world. He wins. Children love that story.
It's also a set of instructions, because Hindus walk around what they love all the time. Around shrines. Around trees.

teach.b: Pradakshina means walking around something holy, clockwise. The direction is inside the word: dakshina means the right hand, the right side.
So you walk keeping the sacred on your right, the side of respect, with the center always in the center.
After darshan at the front of the temple, many people turn and walk around the inner shrine, and many temples build a path for exactly this, a corridor that loops around the sanctum.

Some people do one round, some three, some more, often a number that's meaningful to them or their family. It doesn't stop at the temple walls. People circle the sacred tulsi plant in the courtyard, or a great fig tree.
Some circle whole mountains. At Arunachala, in Tamil Nadu, pilgrims walk all the way around the holy hill, many miles, often barefoot, often at night under the full moon.
Even a Hindu wedding has a circle at its heart: the couple walks around the sacred fire. Why a circle? A straight line goes somewhere else.
A circle keeps coming back to the same center. Every step, the holy is right there beside you, and you can't lose sight of it. And there's Ganesha's point: the thing you circle becomes your world.
That's the teaching your feet are walking: in a Hindu life, God goes at the center, and everything else moves around it.
At the end of home puja, when there's no room to walk, some people simply turn once in place, clockwise. The same act, made small.

how: After darshan, many Hindus walk clockwise around the inner shrine of a temple, keeping the deity on their right, and some also circle sacred trees, the tulsi plant, or holy hills such as Arunachala; at home, some turn once in place at the end of puja.

games.q: you're Ganesha. your brother has flown off to circle the whole world. you have a mouse. what do you do?
o: follow him, slowly, on the mouse.
games.why: he circles Shiva and Parvati and says they're his world. and he wins. pradakshina keeps the holy at the center, the way Ganesha kept his parents.

practice: Stand, if you can, and choose a center: a chair, a table, your corner, or just the spot where you were sitting.

Walk slowly around it clockwise, keeping it on your right, one round, or three if there's room; with no room, turn once in place, and if walking is hard today, trace a slow circle with your hand. Then sit back down at the center.

wordCard.voice: Pradakshina. Walking clockwise around something holy, keeping it on your right, so the center stays the center. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit pradakṣiṇā: moving around with the right side toward the center; circumambulation.
